He may be dead, but none of us ever saw his body. I saw his brother Michael. I was terrified of seeing Curtis himself, but I never did. He may not be dead. He’s lost to me, but I hope he’s not dead. He should be here with me on the road. I hope he’s alive and all right. » Noter la répétition obsessionnelle de dead — six occurrences en six phrases — et l’oscillation entre may be dead et may not be dead. Bankole, la voix douce et grave, demande : « Who have I reminded you of? » Elle secoue la tête : « A boy I knew at home. We were going to get married this year. I don’t even know whether he’s still alive. » Puis l’échange qui apporte l’information la plus révélatrice du chapitre : « You loved him? » — « Yes! We were going to marry and leave home, walk north. We had decided to go this fall. » Et la stupéfaction de Bankole, qui dit tout de ce qu’est devenue la route : « That’s crazy! You intended to walk this road even though you didn’t have to? » Réponse : « Yes. And if we had left earlier, he’d be with me. »

Scene 32 Curtis. The mention of Travis sends her back to Curtis, and she cringes away from thinking of him. Then the chapter’s most painful paragraph, made of a maintained uncertainty: “I’ve thought as little as possible about Curtis Talcott. He isn’t like my brothers. He may be dead, but none of us ever saw his body. I saw his brother Michael. I was terrified of seeing Curtis himself, but I never did. He may not be dead. He’s lost to me, but I hope he’s not dead. He should be here with me on the road. I hope he’s alive and all right.” Note the obsessive repetition of dead — six occurrences in six sentences — and the oscillation between may be dead and may not be dead. Bankole, his voice soft and deep, asks: “Who have I reminded you of?” She shakes her head: “A boy I knew at home. We were going to get married this year. I don’t even know whether he’s still alive.” Then the exchange that yields the chapter’s most revealing information: “You loved him?” — “Yes! We were going to marry and leave home, walk north. We had decided to go this fall.” And Bankole’s astonishment, which says everything about what the road has become: “That’s crazy! You intended to walk this road even though you didn’t have to?” The answer: “Yes. And if we had left earlier, he’d be with me.”

Scène 32 Curtis. « Il est peut-être mort, mais aucun de nous n’a vu son corps » — et : « vous comptiez faire cette route alors que vous n’y étiez pas obligés ? »

Scene 32 Curtis. “He may be dead, but none of us ever saw his body” — and: “you intended to walk this road even though you didn’t have to?”

Scène 33 « Un lien, je suppose ». Bankole s’allonge sur le dos et l’attire près de lui, puis formule ce qui les unit : « We’ve all lost someone. You and I seem to have lost everyone. That’s a bond, I suppose. » Noter la gradation : someone → everyone, et le I suppose qui refuse la solennité. Lauren répond en deux propositions dont la seconde ouvre l’avenir : « A terrible one. But not our only one. » Puis il revient à l’âge, pour la troisième fois : « You’re really eighteen? » — « Yes. As of last month. » — « You look and act years older. » Et la réponse de Lauren est la plus concise qu’elle ait donnée sur elle-même : « This is who I am. » Enfin l’échange final, qui ramène tout le roman en trois répliques : « You were the oldest kid in your family, weren’t you? » — « I nodded. “I had four brothers. They’re all dead.” » — « Yes, » he sighed. « Yes. » Noter le Yes répété : il ne console pas, il enregistre — exactement comme Lauren répondait « Yeah. Yeah. » à Jill au chapitre 20.

Scene 33 “A bond, I suppose.” Bankole lies on his back and draws her down beside him, then formulates what joins them: “We’ve all lost someone. You and I seem to have lost everyone. That’s a bond, I suppose.” Note the gradation: someone → everyone, and the I suppose that refuses solemnity. Lauren answers in two clauses, the second of which opens the future: “A terrible one. But not our only one.” Then he returns to her age for the third time: “You’re really eighteen?” — “Yes. As of last month.” — “You look and act years older.” And Lauren’s reply is the most concise she has given about herself: “This is who I am.” Finally the closing exchange, which brings the whole novel back in three lines: “You were the oldest kid in your family, weren’t you?” — “I nodded. ‘I had four brothers. They’re all dead.’” — “Yes,” he sighed. “Yes.” Note the repeated Yes: he does not console, he registers — exactly as Lauren answered “Yeah. Yeah.” to Jill in Chapter 20.

Scène 33 Le lien. « Toi et moi semblons avoir tout perdu. C’est un lien, je suppose. » — « Un lien terrible. Mais pas le seul. »

Scene 33 The bond. “You and I seem to have lost everyone. That’s a bond, I suppose.” — “A terrible one. But not our only one.”

Scène 34 La leçon devient un office. Mardi 31 août. Lauren résume la journée en une liste de verbes qui n’avaient jamais coexisté dans ce roman : « I’ve spent all of today talking, writing, reading, and making love to Bankole. It seems such a luxury not to have to get up, pack, and walk all day. » Tous sont vautrés autour du campement à reposer des muscles endoloris, à manger et à ne rien faire. Puis la scène qui fonde l’institution : Lauren commence la leçon de lecture de Zahra, et Jill et Allie ont l’air intéressées. Elle les inclut comme si elle l’avait prévu depuis le début. Il s’avère qu’elles savaient lire un peu mais n’avaient jamais appris à écrire. Et vers la fin de la leçon, elle leur lit quelques versets d’Earthseed malgré les gémissements de Harry. Mais c’est la réaction suivante qui change tout : quand Allie proclame qu’elle ne priera jamais aucun dieu du changement, c’est Harry qui la corrige. Zahra et Travis sourient tous les deux ; Bankole les observe tous avec un intérêt apparent. Après quoi Allie se met à poser des questions au lieu de faire des proclamations méprisantes, et, pour l’essentiel, ce sont les autres qui répondent — Travis et Natividad, Harry et Zahra. Une fois, Bankole répond lui-même, développant quelque chose que Lauren lui a dit la veille. Puis il se reprend et paraît un peu gêné. À l’oral : c’est le moment exact où Earthseed cesse d’être la doctrine d’une personne. Lauren se tait et sa religion continue de se transmettre sans elle — y compris par son sceptique le plus bruyant.

Scene 34 The lesson becomes a service. Tuesday 31 August. Lauren sums up the day in a list of verbs that had never coexisted in this novel: “I’ve spent all of today talking, writing, reading, and making love to Bankole. It seems such a luxury not to have to get up, pack, and walk all day.” They all lie sprawled around the campsite resting aching muscles, eating, and doing nothing. Then the scene that founds the institution: Lauren begins Zahra’s reading lesson, and Jill and Allie look interested. She includes them as though she had intended to from the first. It turns out they could read a little but had never learned to write. And towards the end of the lesson, she reads them a few Earthseed verses in spite of Harry’s groans. But it is the next reaction that changes everything: when Allie proclaims that she will never pray to any god of change, it is Harry who corrects her. Zahra and Travis both smile; Bankole watches them all with apparent interest. After that Allie begins to ask questions instead of making scornful proclamations, and for the most part the others answer — Travis and Natividad, Harry and Zahra. Once, Bankole answers himself, expanding on something Lauren told him the day before. Then he catches himself and looks a little embarrassed. In the oral: this is the exact moment Earthseed stops being one person’s doctrine. Lauren falls silent and her religion goes on transmitting itself without her — including through its loudest sceptic.

Scène 34 Sans elle. Allie proclame qu’elle ne priera jamais un dieu du changement — et c’est Harry qui la corrige. Earthseed se transmet désormais sans sa fondatrice.

Scene 34 Without her. Allie proclaims she will never pray to a god of change — and Harry corrects her. Earthseed now transmits itself without its founder.

Scène 35 « Un peu de confusion mystique ». Bankole revient à sa critique de la veille, et il la formule cette fois comme un pronostic technique : « I still think it’s too simple. A lot of it is logical, but it will never work without a sprinkling of mystical confusion. » Le mot est admirable : a sprinkling, une pincée — comme un ingrédient de cuisine manquant dans une recette. Et la réponse de Lauren est la plus désinvolte et la plus grave de tout le roman : « I’ll leave that to my descendants. » Elle concède donc exactement ce qu’il prédit : Earthseed deviendra mystique — mais après elle. Et Butler coupe aussitôt par un geste domestique qui désamorce la solennité : il s’affaire, extrait un sachet d’amandes de son sac, s’en verse dans la main, et fait passer le reste. À l’oral : c’est la seule prophétie du livre que Lauren accepte sans la combattre, et elle la place à une génération de distance.

Scene 35 “A sprinkling of mystical confusion.” Bankole returns to the previous day’s criticism, this time as a technical forecast: “I still think it’s too simple. A lot of it is logical, but it will never work without a sprinkling of mystical confusion.” The word is admirable: a sprinkling, a pinch — like a missing ingredient in a recipe. And Lauren’s answer is the most offhand and the gravest in the novel: “I’ll leave that to my descendants.” She therefore concedes exactly what he predicts: Earthseed will become mystical — but after her. And Butler cuts away at once with a domestic gesture that defuses the solemnity: he busies himself, digs a bag of almonds out of his pack, pours some into his hand, and passes the rest around. In the oral: this is the only prophecy in the book that Lauren accepts without fighting it, and she places it a generation away.

Scène 35 La pincée. « Cela ne marchera jamais sans une pincée de confusion mystique. » — « Je laisserai ça à mes descendants. »

Scene 35 The pinch. “It will never work without a sprinkling of mystical confusion.” — “I’ll leave that to my descendants.”

Scène 36 Ce qui est devenu normal. Juste avant la nuit, une bataille au fusil commence du côté de l’autoroute. Ils ne voient rien, mais cessent de parler et se couchent. Avec des balles qui volent, il semblait préférable de rester bas. Le combat a un rythme : les tirs commencent et s’arrêtent, s’éloignent, puis reviennent. Lauren est de garde, donc elle doit rester vigilante — mais, dans cette tempête de bruit, rien ne bouge près d’eux sauf les arbres dans la brise du soir. Et vient le contraste, en une phrase : « It looked so peaceful, and yet people out there were trying to kill each other, and no doubt succeeding. » Puis la dernière phrase du chapitre, qui est l’une des plus importantes du roman pour l’oral : « Strange how normal it’s become for us to lie on the ground and listen while nearby, people try to kill each other. » Noter que le chapitre le plus heureux du livre — deux jours de repos, une leçon de lecture, un amour qui commence — se termine couché par terre pendant une fusillade, et que ce qui frappe Lauren n’est pas la fusillade mais sa propre accoutumance. C’est l’exact contraire d’un chapitre de repos : c’est un chapitre qui mesure ce que le voyage leur a déjà coûté.

Scene 36 What has become normal. Just before nightfall, a gun battle begins over toward the highway. They can see nothing, but they stop talking and lie down. With bullets flying, it seemed best to keep low. The fight has a rhythm: the shooting starts and stops, moves away, then comes back. Lauren is on watch, so she has to stay alert — but in this storm of noise, nothing moves near them except the trees in the evening breeze. And then the contrast, in one sentence: “It looked so peaceful, and yet people out there were trying to kill each other, and no doubt succeeding.” Then the chapter’s last sentence, one of the novel’s most important for the oral: “Strange how normal it’s become for us to lie on the ground and listen while nearby, people try to kill each other.” Note that the book’s happiest chapter — two days of rest, a reading lesson, a love beginning — ends lying on the ground during a firefight, and that what strikes Lauren is not the firefight but her own habituation. It is the exact opposite of a rest chapter: it is a chapter that measures what the journey has already cost them.

Scène 36 L’accoutumance. « Étrange comme c’est devenu normal, pour nous, de rester couchés par terre à écouter des gens essayer de s’entretuer tout près. »

Scene 36 Habituation. “Strange how normal it’s become for us to lie on the ground and listen while nearby, people try to kill each other.”

Ch. 21, épigrapheCh. 21, epigraph"To shape God, Shape Self."
ProcédéDevice

Chiasme avec reprise du verbe ; majuscule au second Shape, qui en fait un impératif.

A chiasmus repeating the verb; a capital on the second Shape, turning it into an imperative.

EffetEffect

Quatre mots qui inversent l’ordre des opérations du chapitre 18. Là, Shape God était l’aboutissement ; ici, il devient le but, et le moyen est le travail sur soi. Avec les deux vers qui précèdent — The Self must create / Its own reasons for being — on obtient la seule page franchement existentialiste d’Earthseed, et Bankole la reconnaîtra comme telle dans ce même chapitre (« Buddhism, existentialism, Sufism »). Le placement est décisif : c’est le chapitre où Lauren dit « all that I am now is Earthseed ». La fondatrice et la doctrine deviennent le même objet — ce qui est la réussite du verset et, simultanément, son danger : une religion qui exige qu’on se façonne soi-même aboutit ici à une femme de dix-huit ans qui n’a plus d’autre contenu qu’elle. À l’oral, poser la question sans la trancher : est-ce un accomplissement ou une perte ?

Four words that invert the order of operations from Chapter 18. There, Shape God was the outcome; here it becomes the aim, and the means is work on the self. With the two preceding lines — The Self must create / Its own reasons for being — this is Earthseed’s one frankly existentialist page, and Bankole will recognise it as such in this very chapter (“Buddhism, existentialism, Sufism”). The placement is decisive: this is the chapter in which Lauren says “all that I am now is Earthseed”. Founder and doctrine become the same object — which is the verse’s success and, simultaneously, its danger: a religion that demands you shape yourself produces here an eighteen-year-old woman who has no other content left. In the oral, put the question without settling it: is that an achievement or a loss?

Religion & beliefIsolation & alienation
À l’oralIn the oral « A religion that tells you to shape yourself produces a founder with nothing left in her but the religion. »“A religion that tells you to shape yourself produces a founder with nothing left in her but the religion.”
Ch. 21, à BankoleCh. 21, to Bankole"Stumbling across the truth isn’t the same as making things up."
ProcédéDevice

Maxime en opposition de gérondifs ; verbe d’accident (stumbling) revendiqué comme preuve.

A maxim opposing two gerunds; a verb of accident (stumbling) claimed as proof.

EffetEffect

C’est la défense permanente d’Earthseed contre l’accusation d’invention, et elle est construite sur une concession : Lauren ne revendique ni révélation ni recherche méthodique, mais un trébuchement — c’est-à-dire le mode d’accès le plus humble possible à une vérité qui, elle, existait déjà. C’est la version compacte du caillou posé sur la table au chapitre 18 (« would that mean I’d made up its contents? »). Deux prolongements pour une copie forte. D’abord l’aveu qui suit immédiatement : « I wondered how many times and ways I would have to say this to new people » — la fondatrice sait déjà qu’elle passera sa vie à répéter cette phrase, ce qui la transforme en apôtre fatiguée avant d’avoir dix convertis. Ensuite, le fait que Bankole ne soit pas convaincu : il répond en classant Earthseed parmi le bouddhisme et l’existentialisme. Butler laisse donc l’objection debout.

This is Earthseed’s permanent defence against the charge of invention, and it is built on a concession: Lauren claims neither revelation nor methodical search, but a stumble — the humblest possible mode of access to a truth that already existed. It is the compact version of the stone on the table in Chapter 18 (“would that mean I’d made up its contents?”). Two extensions for a strong essay. First, the admission that immediately follows: “I wondered how many times and ways I would have to say this to new people” — the founder already knows she will spend her life repeating this sentence, which makes her a weary apostle before she has ten converts. Second, the fact that Bankole is not convinced: he answers by filing Earthseed among Buddhism and existentialism. Butler therefore leaves the objection standing.

Religion & beliefPower & control
À l’oralIn the oral « She claims a stumble, not a revelation — the humblest possible claim, and the hardest to refute. »“She claims a stumble, not a revelation — the humblest possible claim, and the hardest to refute.”
Ch. 21, la prophétie de BankoleCh. 21, Bankole’s prophecy"… more complicated, more open to interpretation, more mystical, and more comforting."
ProcédéDevice

Gradation de quatre comparatifs ; prédiction formulée par un sceptique bienveillant.

A gradation of four comparatives; a prediction made by a sympathetic sceptic.

EffetEffect

Les quatre comparatifs vont du neutre au fatal : complicated et open to interpretation sont des constats sociologiques ; mystical est déjà une trahison des principes ; comforting est l’exact contraire de ce qu’Earthseed prétend être (au ch. 18, Lauren concédait elle-même : « Your stuff isn’t very comforting » — « It is after a while »). Lauren proteste — « Not around me they won’t! » — et Bankole répond : « With you or without you, they will », puis retourne le credo : si Dieu est Changement, Earthseed peut changer, et si elle dure, elle changera. C’est la critique interne la plus forte du roman : la doctrine contient le principe de sa propre déformation. Et Lauren finit par capituler avec élégance le lendemain : « I’ll leave that to my descendants ». À l’oral, citation idéale pour toute question sur l’avenir d’Earthseed ou sur la fiabilité de l’espoir dans ce livre.

The four comparatives move from neutral to fatal: complicated and open to interpretation are sociological observations; mystical is already a betrayal of the principles; comforting is the exact opposite of what Earthseed claims to be (in ch. 18 Lauren herself conceded: “Your stuff isn’t very comforting” — “It is after a while”). Lauren protests — “Not around me they won’t!” — and Bankole answers: “With you or without you, they will”, then turns the creed over: if God is Change, Earthseed can change, and if it lasts, it will. This is the novel’s strongest internal criticism: the doctrine contains the principle of its own deformation. And Lauren capitulates elegantly the next day: “I’ll leave that to my descendants”. In the oral, an ideal quotation for any question on Earthseed’s future or on the reliability of hope in this book.

Religion & beliefPower & control
À l’oralIn the oral « Earthseed will not be destroyed by its enemies but softened by its believers — and its own creed guarantees it. »“Earthseed will not be destroyed by its enemies but softened by its believers — and its own creed guarantees it.”
Ch. 21, « how serious are you? »Ch. 21, “how serious are you?”"What I am now, all that I am now is Earthseed."
ProcédéDevice

Reprise correctrice (what I am → all that I am) ; identification pure, sans verbe d’opinion.

A self-correcting repetition (what I am → all that I am); pure identification, with no verb of opinion.

EffetEffect

La phrase arrive au terme d’une progression en trois pertes : quand son père a disparu, Earthseed l’a maintenue debout ; quand sa communauté et sa famille ont été anéanties, « I still had Earthseed » ; maintenant, elle est Earthseed. Le mouvement va du soutien à la possession, puis à l’identité — et le correctif all that ferme la porte à toute autre définition d’elle-même. Deux lectures sont possibles et l’oral gagne à les tenir ensemble. Lecture héroïque : une femme qui a tout perdu a converti sa perte en œuvre, et c’est la seule victoire disponible dans ce monde. Lecture inquiétante : une fille de dix-huit ans n’a plus de contenu propre, et Bankole le sent, puisqu’il répond en refusant la doctrine pour nommer la personne — « What you are now is a very unusual young woman ». Noter enfin les points de suspension après « When my father… disappeared » : un seul mot la fait encore hésiter, et ce n’est pas un mot d’Earthseed.

The sentence comes at the end of a progression through three losses: when her father disappeared, Earthseed kept her going; when her community and family were wiped out, “I still had Earthseed”; now, she is Earthseed. The movement runs from support to possession to identity — and the corrective all that closes the door on any other definition of herself. Two readings are available and the oral gains by holding both. The heroic reading: a woman who has lost everything has converted her loss into a work, the only victory available in this world. The disquieting reading: an eighteen-year-old has no content of her own left, and Bankole senses it, since he answers by refusing the doctrine in order to name the person — “What you are now is a very unusual young woman”. Note finally the ellipsis after “When my father… disappeared”: one word still makes her hesitate, and it is not an Earthseed word.

À l’oralIn the oral « He answers a statement of doctrine by naming the person — the only person in the book who does. »“He answers a statement of doctrine by naming the person — the only character in the book who does.”
Ch. 21, fin du chapitreCh. 21, end of chapter"Strange how normal it’s become for us to lie on the ground and listen…"
ProcédéDevice

Constat d’habituation en clausule ; adjectif normal appliqué à une fusillade.

A statement of habituation as clausula; the adjective normal applied to a firefight.

EffetEffect

La phrase complète est : « … while nearby, people try to kill each other ». Ce qui étonne Lauren n’est pas la violence mais sa propre adaptation à elle — et c’est précisément ce qui fait de cette fin le contraire d’un chapitre de repos. Mesurer le trajet : au chapitre 16, elle passait trois heures de garde « weary, terrifying », en sueur froide, à désirer des murs ; ici, elle est de garde pendant une bataille et remarque que les arbres bougent dans la brise du soir. Le roman a donc consacré son chapitre le plus heureux — deux jours de repos, une leçon de lecture, un premier amour — à faire apparaître le coût du voyage sous la forme d’une accoutumance. À l’oral, c’est la citation à placer contre toute lecture optimiste de la fin du livre : le groupe progresse, s’organise, s’aime — et s’habitue.

The full sentence is: “… while nearby, people try to kill each other”. What astonishes Lauren is not the violence but her own adaptation to it — and that is precisely what makes this ending the opposite of a rest chapter. Measure the distance travelled: in Chapter 16 she spent three hours on watch “weary, terrifying”, in a cold sweat, longing for walls; here she is on watch during a battle and notices that the trees are moving in the evening breeze. The novel has therefore used its happiest chapter — two days of rest, a reading lesson, a first love — to reveal the cost of the journey in the form of habituation. In the oral, this is the quotation to set against any optimistic reading of the book’s ending: the group advances, organises itself, loves — and gets used to it.
